analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers have the IRS prepare and file their taxes for free, using data the government already has.
analysis.headline: A bill to let the IRS prepare and file taxes for free for simple returns was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the IRS build free online tax filing software, pull in wage and other income data the government already receives so returns are largely pre-filled, and let people with simple finances have the IRS prepare their return entirely — at no charge. It would also bar the Treasury Department from signing any deal restricting the IRS from offering these services. A separate portal would let people who do not normally file claim the Earned Income Tax Credit and child tax credit with minimal paperwork. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers — especially low- and middle-income people who pay for commercial tax software or preparers, and the roughly one in five eligible workers who never claim the Earned Income Tax Credit. They could file free with pre-filled data, and non-filers could claim credits through a simple portal without a full return. All taxpayers would gain a no-fee option for simple returns, prepared by the IRS itself.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the IRS to build free online tax preparation and filing software for taxable years after 2022, with no fee charged to any participant.
Requires the IRS to prefill returns with wage and other third-party information it already receives, so taxpayers are not re-entering data employers and banks already reported.
Creates a simplified portal letting people who normally do not file claim the Earned Income Tax Credit and child tax credit without reporting extra income data.

Lets taxpayers elect to have simple returns prepared entirely by the IRS, initially for those taking the standard deduction with only wage, interest, or dividend income, with eligibility expandable later.
Bans the Treasury from any agreement restricting the IRS's right to prepare or file returns, heading off contractual limits on a public filing option.

Requires identity verification that works for most taxpayers including EITC-eligible households, with backup in-person options, plus a public outreach campaign and coordination with states so one filing covers federal and state returns.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies would lose customers who switch to free government filing, and taxpayers fund the new IRS programs through appropriations. Taxpayers remain responsible for the accuracy of their own returns, as the bill states.

drawbacks.text: Building and running a free IRS filing system requires new federal spending, which the bill authorizes as 'such sums as may be necessary' through fiscal 2026 without naming a funding source.

The IRS-prepared-return option is initially limited to people with simple returns (wages, interest, or dividends, no business income), so its benefit reaches only a subset of taxpayers at first, with expansion left to the Treasury Secretary's discretion.

Identity verification could block some eligible people — especially those without internet, credit histories, or stable housing — which the bill tries to mitigate with secondary and in-person verification options and annual reporting on pass rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to taxpayers are concrete and immediate: free filing, prefilled data, and a portal that gets unclaimed credits into people's hands. The costs are real but bounded: tax preparation companies lose the revenue they now earn from filings the government could do for free, and taxpayers must fund the IRS program to build and run it. Identity verification and outreach, which the bill addresses in detail, are the main implementation risks. Nothing in the record suggests the design is unsound; the bill simply never received a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced it in July 2022, the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, and it sat there without a hearing or vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 12, 2022, with 22 cosponsors — 20 Senate Democrats and both independents.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the committee took no further action on it.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or House action occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paid tax preparation companies keep the filing fees taxpayers would have saved, and no agreement restricts the IRS from offering its own service.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 22 cosponsors.

for.name: 22 senators (20 Democrats, 2 independents)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Sen. Angus King (I-ME).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 12, 2022 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Tax preparation industry
against.role: Commercial tax software and preparation companies
against.what_they_did: Long opposed IRS free filing and return-preparation by the government, which would compete with their paid services.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; none of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software companies (e.g. paid e-filing providers)
industries.note: The bill would give taxpayers a free government alternative to paid preparation and bar the IRS from signing any agreement restricting that service. Its core business — charging individuals, especially lower-income filers, to file returns the government could largely pre-fill — would shrink.

industries.industry: Payroll and information-return filers (employers, banks, brokers)
industries.note: The bill moves information-return deadlines to January 31 and removes extensions, and requires wage data to reach the IRS by February 15, giving employers and financial firms less time to report but enabling pre-filled returns for taxpayers.
